overview: I invoke that energy which is the master of all my senses. Please come and be present before us, and listen to what we are saying. The supreme consciousness is always present — but are we aware of it? By reciting this mantra we make ourselves aware of it. Then: may that supreme consciousness flow through me. Just as current flowing through a bulb lights it up, the intellect is the bulb and consciousness is the current. When that current flows, the intellect is illumined.

universalReflection: Before we speak, we ask to be worth listening to. Every act of learning begins by admitting we do not yet know.

parallels.text: Waheguru is a focal word around which every activity of a Sikh revolves. Waheguru Simran serves as a constant expression of internal awareness of the Divine, and the term is carried into daily vocabulary as a social expression of Divine consciousness.

overview: We meditate on THAT divine, life-sustaining, resplendent effulgence, pervading the gross, the subtle and the causal. May THAT supreme intelligence illuminate our intellects.
structure: The Gayatri has three parts — adoration, meditation, and prayer. First the Divine is praised, then meditated upon in reverence, and finally an appeal is made to awaken and strengthen the intellect, the discriminating faculty of the human being. (Sri Sathya Sai Baba)

wordMeanings.meaning: causal / sky / future / deep sleep state

universalReflection: The prayer does not ask for wealth, safety or victory. It asks only that our thinking be made clear. Everything else follows from that.

quotes.text: The Gayatri is considered the essence of the Vedas. Veda means knowledge, and this prayer fosters and sharpens the knowledge-yielding faculty.
The Gayatri is a universal prayer enshrined in the Vedas. It is addressed to the Immanent and Transcendent Divine, given the name 'Savita' — that from which all this is born.

parallels.text: We pray to You alone and seek help from You alone. Show us the righteous path — the path of those blessed with Your light and grace.
Surrender to Buddha — enlightened awareness. Surrender to Dhamma — inner righteousness. Surrender to Sangha — collective consciousness.
Guide me on the path of righteousness; show me Your way, which is straight, noble and perfect.
Our eyes may see indecent things, but our hearts should be free of impurity. Our ears may hear what is profane, but our hearts should perceive nothing unholy.

note: The final line is chanted three times.

overview: May the people be governed and nourished well by those who rule. May there be happiness and peace among them. May those who govern the land tread the path of justice. May knowledge, and those who carry knowledge, ever be well. May all the worlds be happy.

wordMeanings.meaning: for the people, the common citizens

universalReflection: A prayer for good government, honest leadership, protected knowledge and a cared-for earth — asked for everyone, not for oneself. It is one of the few prayers in any tradition that contains no request for the person praying.
teachingNote: In late 2008, Bhagawan directed that we should henceforward chant Samasta Lokāḥ Sukhino Bhavantu rather than Lokāḥ Samastā Sukhino Bhavantu. The earlier form referred only to this world; the revised form refers to all the worlds, and is broader in outlook.

quotes.text: Peace is a shoreless ocean. It is the light that illumines the world. Having peace amounts to having everything. It confers knowledge of both this world and the other.

parallels.text: The root of the word Islam is silm, meaning peace. A hadith records that a Muslim is one from whose tongue and hands people live safely — one who harms no one by word or deed.
Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way.
The Giver of peace is eternally blissful. Through the Guru's teachings, we are absorbed in intuitive peace.

overview: Whichever sound or word has been corrupted, whichever timing has run too long or too short — for all of that, please forgive me, O Deva Nārāyaṇa; my salutations to you. Whether the fault was in visarga, in bindu, in timing, in word or in syllable, whether it was longer or shorter than it should have been, forgive me, O Sāyīśvara. I have committed offences by the thousand, day and night — knowing me as your servant, forgive me, O Sāyīśvara. Elsewhere I have no refuge; you alone are my refuge. Out of your compassion, protect me, protect me, O Sāyīśvara. Hariḥ Om — that is the truth. This is all surrendered at the feet of Sāyīśvara.

wordMeanings.meaning: phonetic marks of correct Vedic pronunciation

universalReflection: This prayer does not ask to be spared the consequence of error — it asks only to be forgiven for having erred while trying. It trusts that sincere effort, offered honestly, is enough.

quotes.text: Forbearance and forgiveness are the qualities that should be fostered by all individuals. You must be able to forgive even your enemies.

parallels.text: Forgive others not because they deserve forgiveness, but because you deserve peace.
Forgive them, even if they are not sorry.
For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.

overview: The one who understands the flowers (puṣpam) of the waters (āpaḥ), and their relationship to the moon (candramāḥ), reaches the highest abode. Bhagawan Sri Sathya Sai Baba explains that āpaḥ — the waters of life — is Love. Read this way, the hymn says: the one who understands the inner significance of Love, and its relationship to the mind, reaches the highest abode. This is all there is to know — the one illumined by Love attains the highest abode.

overview: Śiva means positive, auspicious, serene — the one who is not affected by any kind of negativity. Upāsana comes from upa (close) and āsana (sitting): sitting close to Him. Śivopāsana therefore means being rooted in the consciousness and awareness of Shiva. That consciousness is fundamentally the breath of the entire universe; when we breathe in and breathe out Shiva, we are in Śivopāsana.
structure: Holding the liṅgam, twenty-two mantras consecrate and install it. The five faces of the liṅgam are then worshipped in turn: Sadyojāta facing west, Vāmadeva north, Aghora south, Tatpuruṣa east, and Īśāna facing upward.

verses.meaning: All mantras end with an invocation of peace, made for the purpose of averting all evil. It allows one to be at peace with oneself and the universe, to have calmness and concentration. The three repetitions address the three sources of disturbance: ādhyātmika (from within oneself — mind, body, emotions), ādhibhautika (from other living beings) and ādhidaivika (from natural and cosmic forces).

overview: The word kṛmi works on two levels at once, and this dual meaning is the heart of the hymn's relevance. Literally, it was chanted with precise intention toward the elimination of pests, parasites and disease-causing organisms that threatened crops, livestock and human health. Read inwardly, kṛmi represents anything that eats away at our wellbeing from within — the repetitive thought patterns that erode our peace, the jealousy, anger, fear and greed that infect relationships, the toxic habits that quietly consume our health and time, and the disharmony that spreads through a community like a contagion.
teachingNote: When first translated into English these words can sound startling, even violent — germs are 'slain', their chieftains and parents 'annihilated'. In the ancient world, long before microscopes, the seers already understood that the body, the home and the environment could be invaded by unseen harmful forces. They called these kṛmi, and the language of the hymn is the language of driving them out.

universalReflection: Just as we keep our homes physically clean, our ancestors understood that we must also keep our minds, our words and our shared environment clean — free from the unseen, corrosive forces of negativity. This is as relevant in a Cape Town apartment or a Durban household today as it was in a forest ashram thousands of years ago. Whether someone calls it prayer, meditation, affirmation or sound therapy, the underlying human need — to protect our inner and outer world from what diminishes it — is universal.

verses.devanagari: ओ-न्तत्पुरु॑षाय वि॒द्महे॑ चक्रतु॒ण्डाय॑ धीमहि । तन्नो॑ नन्दिः प्रचो॒दया᳚त् ॥
verses.iast: tatpuru̍ṣāya vi̱dmahe̍ cakratu̱ṇḍāya̍ dhīmahi । tanno̍ nandiḥ(f) praco̱dayā̎t ॥ 4 ॥
verses.meaning: We know that Puruṣa; we meditate on Cakratuṇḍa. May Nandi impel us.

verses.devanagari: ओ-न्तत्पुरु॑षाय वि॒द्महे॑ महासे॒नाय॑ धीमहि । तन्न-ष्षण्मुखः प्रचो॒दया᳚त् ॥
verses.iast: tatpuru̍ṣāya vi̱dmahe̍ mahāse̱nāya̍ dhīmahi । tannaṣ ṣaṇmukhaḥ(f) praco̱dayā̎t ॥ 5 ॥
verses.meaning: We know that Puruṣa; we meditate on Mahāsena, the great commander. May Ṣaṇmukha, the six-faced one, impel us.

verses.devanagari: ओ-न्तत्पुरु॑षाय वि॒द्महे॑ सुवर्णप॒क्षाय॑ धीमहि । तन्नो॑ गरुडः प्रचो॒दया᳚त् ॥
verses.iast: tatpuru̍ṣāya vi̱dmahe̍ suvarṇapa̱kṣāya̍ dhīmahi । tanno̍ garuḍaḥ(f) praco̱dayā̎t ॥ 6 ॥
verses.meaning: We know that Puruṣa; we meditate on the golden-winged one. May Garuḍa impel us.

verses.devanagari: ॐ-वेँ॒दा॒त्म॒नाय॑ वि॒द्महे॑ हिरण्यग॒र्भाय॑ धीमहि । तन्नो॑ ब्रह्मः प्रचो॒दया᳚त् ॥
verses.iast: ve̱dā̱tma̱nāya̍ vi̱dmahe̍ hiraṇyaga̱rbhāya̍ dhīmahi । tanno̎ brahma praco̱dayā̎t ॥ 7 ॥
verses.meaning: We know the Self of the Vedas; we meditate on Hiraṇyagarbha, the golden womb. May Brahmā impel us.

verses.devanagari: ओ-न्ना॒रा॒य॒णाय॑ वि॒द्महे॑ वासुदे॒वाय॑ धीमहि । तन्नो॑ विष्णुः प्रचो॒दया᳚त् ॥
verses.iast: nā̱rā̱ya̱ṇāya̍ vi̱dmahe̍ vā̱su̱de̱vāya̍ dhīmahi । tanno̍ viṣṇuḥ(f) praco̱dayā̎t ॥ 8 ॥
verses.meaning: We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate on Vāsudeva. May Viṣṇu impel us.

verses.devanagari: ॐ-वँ॒ज्र॒न॒खाय वि॒द्महे॑ तीक्ष्णद॒ग्ग्-ष्ट्राय॑ धीमहि । तन्नो॑ नारसिग्ंहः प्रचो॒दया᳚त् ॥
verses.iast: va̱jra̱na̱khāya̍ vi̱dmahe̍ tīkṣṇada̱gṁṣṭrāya̍ dhīmahi । tanno̍ nārasigṁhaḥ(f) praco̱dayā̎t ॥ 9 ॥
verses.meaning: We know the one with adamantine claws; we meditate on the sharp-fanged one. May Narasiṁha impel us.

verses.devanagari: ओ-म्भा॒स्क॒राय॑ वि॒द्महे॑ महद्द्युतिक॒राय॑ धीमहि । तन्नो॑ आदित्यः प्रचो॒दया᳚त् ॥
verses.iast: bhā̱ska̱rāya̍ vi̱dmahe̍ mahadyutika̱rāya̍ dhīmahi । tanno̍ | ādityaḥ(f) praco̱dayā̎t ॥ 10 ॥
verses.meaning: We know the light-maker; we meditate on the one of great radiance. May Āditya, the sun, impel us.

verses.devanagari: ॐ-वैँ॒श्वा॒न॒राय॑ वि॒द्महे॑ लाली॒लाय धीमहि । तन्नो॑ अग्निः प्रचो॒दया᳚त् ॥
verses.iast: vai̱śvā̱na̱rāya̍ vi̱dmahe̍ lālī̱lāya dhīmahi । tanno̍ | agniḥ(f) praco̱dayā̎t ॥ 11 ॥
verses.meaning: We know Vaiśvānara, the fire in all beings; we meditate on Lālīla. May Agni impel us.

verses.devanagari: ओ-ङ्का॒त्या॒य॒नाय॑ वि॒द्महे॑ कन्यकु॒मारि॑ धीमहि । तन्नो॑ दुर्गिः प्रचो॒दया᳚त् ॥
verses.iast: kā̱tyā̱ya̱nāya̍ vi̱dmahe̍ kanyaku̱māri̍ dhīmahi । tanno̍ durgiḥ(f) praco̱dayā̎t ॥ 12 ॥
verses.meaning: We know Kātyāyanī; we meditate on Kanyākumārī. May Durgā impel us.

verses.iast: oṁ sā̱yī̱śva̱rāya̍ vi̱dmahe̍ satyade̱vāya̍ dhīmahi । tanna̍s sarvaḥ(f) praco̱dayā̎t ॥ 18 ॥
verses.meaning: We know Sāyīśvara; we meditate on Satyadeva, the God of Truth. May that All impel us.

verses.iast: ॥ oṁ | śānti̱ś śānti̱ś śānti̍ḥ ॥
verses.meaning: Om. Peace, peace, peace.

overview: Every verse follows the same three-part Gāyatrī pattern: we know (vidmahe) one name of the Divine, we meditate (dhīmahi) on another, and we ask that a third impel or illumine us (pracodayāt). Only the names change — Rudra, Danti, Nandi, Ṣaṇmukha, Garuḍa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Narasiṁha, Āditya, Agni, Durgā, and finally Sāyīśvara as Satyadeva, the God of Truth.
structure: The pattern is the same as the Gāyatrī Mantra itself — adoration, meditation, then the appeal that the intellect be awakened — repeated for each form of the Divine in turn.

wordMeanings.meaning: may it impel, may it illumine
all the deities, every form of the Divine

universalReflection: Thirteen names, one prayer. Each verse asks for exactly the same thing — that the mind be awakened — and only the name it is addressed to changes. The form of address turns out to matter less than what is being asked for.

note: The food prayer is taken from two verses of the divine scripture of the Bhagavad Gita.

verses.iast: Brahmārpaṇaṃ Brahmahavir-brahmāgnau Brahmaṇāhutaṃ |
verses.meaning: The fire in the belly consumes, and that is the Brahman. The material is Brahman, the one who is consuming is Brahman, it is consumed by the Brahman, it is converted into the energy of the Brahman, and that energy helps us to do the work of the Brahman.

words.meaning: consumed by the Brahman, the fire within me

verses.iast: Brahmaiva Tena Gantavyam Brahmakarma Samadhinā ||
Ahaṃ Vaiśvānaro Bhūtvā Prāṇinān Dehamāśritaḥ |
verses.meaning: I am going to take what you have provided, both solid and liquid, and convert that into the life force within you. I will balance the life forces within you.

words.meaning: present within you as the fire named Vaiśvānara
present in all the bodies of all beings

verses.iast: Prāṇāpāna Samāyuktaḥ Pacāmyannañ Caturvidhaṃ ||

overview: The fire in the belly consumes, and that is the Brahman. Consuming the Brahman Himself, the energy that is produced is the Brahman, and that energy is used to do the work of the Brahman. The second verse is the Lord's own answer: I am present within you as the fire named Vaiśvānara, present in the bodies of all beings, and I convert what you take — both solid and liquid — into the life force within you.

wordMeanings.meaning: consumed by the Brahman, the fire within me
present within you as the fire named Vaiśvānara
present in all the bodies of all beings

universalReflection: Said before eating, it removes every separation in the act: what is eaten, the one eating, the fire that digests and the work the energy goes on to do are all named as one and the same thing.

note: Chanted in two anuvākas, opened and closed by the same śānti. The verse numbers restart at 1 in the second anuvāka, as the booklet prints them.

verses.iast: ॥ śrī̱ sā̱yī̱śva̱rā̱ya namaḥ । hari̍ḥ | oṁ ॥

verses.devanagari: ओ-न्तच्छं॒-योँरावृ॑णीमहे । गा॒तुं-यँ॒ज्ञाय॑ । गा॒तुं-यँ॒ज्ञप॑तये । दैवी᳚ स्व॒स्तिर॑स्तु नः । स्व॒स्तिर्मानु॑षेभ्यः । ऊ॒र्ध्व-ञ्जि॑गातु भेष॒जम् । श-न्नो॑ अस्तु द्वि॒पदे᳚ । श-ञ्चतु॑ष्पदे ।
verses.iast: oṁ | tacha̱ṁi yorāvṛ̍ṇīmahe । gā̱tuṁi ya̱jñāya̍ । gā̱tuṁi ya̱jña pa̍taye । daivī̎ sva̱stira̍stu naḥ । sva̱stir mānu̍ṣebhyaḥ । ū̱rdhvañ ji̍gātu bheṣa̱jam । śan no̍ | astu dvi̱pade̎ । śañ catu̍ṣpade ॥

verses.devanagari: ॐ शान्ति॒-श्शान्ति॒-श्शान्तिः॑ ॥
verses.iast: oṁ | śāntiś śāntiś śānti̍ḥ ॥

verses.devanagari: स॒हस्र॑शीर् षा॒ पुरु॑षः । स॒ह॒स्रा॒क्ष-स्स॒हस्र॑पात् । स भूमिं॑-विँ॒श्वतो॑ वृ॒त्वा । अत्य॑तिष्ठद्दशाङ्गु॒लम् ॥
verses.iast: sa̱hasra̍śīr·ṣā̱ puru̍ṣaḥ । sa̱ha̱srā̱kṣas sa̱hasra̍pāt । sa bhūmi̍ṁu vi̱śvato̍ vṛ̱tvā । atya̍tiṣṭhaddaśāṅgu̱lam ॥ 1 ॥

verses.devanagari: पुरु॑ष ए॒वेदग्ं सर्वम्᳚ । यद्भू॒तं-यँच्च॒ भव्यम्᳚ । उ॒तामृ॑त॒त्व स्येशा॑नः । यदन्ने॑नाति॒रोह॑ति ॥
verses.iast: puru̍ṣa | e̱veda gṁ sarvam̎ । yadbhū̱taṁi yacca̱ bhavyam̎ । u̱tāmṛ̍ta̱tvasyeśā̍naḥ । yadanne̍nāti̱roha̍ti ॥ 2 ॥

verses.devanagari: ए॒तावा॑नस्य महि॒मा । अतो॒ ज्यायाग्॑श्च॒ पूरु॑षः । पादो᳚-ऽस्य॒ विश्वा॑ भू॒तानि॑ । त्रि॒पाद॑स्या॒मृत॑-न्दि॒वि ॥
verses.iast: e̱tāvā̍nasya mahi̱mā । ato̱ jyāyā̍gśca̱ pūru̍ṣaḥ । pādo̎'sya̱ viśvā̍ bhū̱tāni̍ । tri̱pāda̍syā̱mṛta̍n di̱vi ॥ 3 ॥

verses.devanagari: त्रि॒पादू॒र्ध्व उदै॒त्पुरु॑षः । पादो᳚-ऽस्ये॒हा-ऽऽभ॑वा॒त्पुनः॑ । ततो॒ विष्व॒ङ् व्य॑क्रामत् । सा॒श॒ना॒न॒श॒ने अ॒भि ॥
verses.iast: tri̱pādū̱rdhva | udai̱tpuru̍ṣaḥ । pādo̎'sye̱hā''bha̍vā̱tpuna̍ḥ । tato̱ viṣva̱ṁu vya̍krāmat । sā̱śa̱nā̱na̱śa̱ne | a̱bhi ॥ 4 ॥

verses.devanagari: तस्मा᳚द्वि॒राड॑जायत । वि॒राजो॒ अधि॒ पूरु॑षः । स जा॒तो अत्य॑रिच्यत । प॒श्चाद्भूमि॒मथो॑ पु॒रः ॥
verses.iast: tasmā̎dvi̱rāḍa̍jāyata । vi̱rājo̱ | adhi̱ pūru̍ṣaḥ । sa jā̱to | atya̍ricyata । pa̱ścādbhūmi̱matho̍ pu̱raḥ ॥ 5 ॥

verses.devanagari: यत्पुरु॑षेण ह॒विषा᳚ । दे॒वा य॒ज्ञमत॑न्वत । व॒स॒न्तो अ॑स्यासी॒दाज्यम्᳚ । ग्री॒ष्म इ॒ध्मश्श॒रध्ध॒विः ॥
verses.iast: yatpuru̍ṣeṇa ha̱viṣā̎ । de̱vā ya̱jñamata̍nvata । va̱sa̱nto | a̍syā''sī̱dājyam̎ । grī̱ṣma | i̱dhmaś śa̱raddha̱viḥ ॥ 6 ॥

verses.devanagari: स॒प्तास्या॑सन्परि॒धयः॑ । त्रि-स्स॒प्त स॒मिधः॑ कृ॒ताः । दे॒वा यद्य॒ज्ञ-न्त॑न्वा॒नाः । अब॑ध्न॒न्-पुरु॑ष-म्प॒शुम् ॥
verses.iast: sa̱ptāsyā̍sanpari̱dhaya̍ḥ । tris sa̱pta sa̱midha̍ḥ kṛ̱tāḥ । de̱vā yadya̱jñan ta̍nvā̱nāḥ । aba̍dhna̱npuru̍ṣam pa̱śum ॥ 7 ॥

verses.devanagari: तं-यँ॒ज्ञ-म्ब॒र्॒हिषि॒ प्रौक्षन्॑ । पुरु॑ष-ञ्जा॒तम॑ग्र॒तः । तेन॑ दे॒वा अय॑जन्त । सा॒ध्या ऋष॑यश्च॒ ये ॥
verses.iast: taṁi ya̱jñam ba̱rhiṣi̱ praukṣan̍ । puru̍ṣañ jā̱tama̍gra̱taḥ । tena̍ de̱vā | aya̍janta । sā̱dhyā | ṛṣa̍yaś ca̱ ye ॥ 8 ॥

verses.devanagari: तस्मा᳚द्य॒ज्ञाथ्स॑र्व॒हुतः॑ । सम्भृ॑त-म्पृषदा॒ज्यम् । प॒शूग्-स्ताग्-श्च॑क्रे वाय॒व्यान्॑ । आ॒र॒ण्यान्-ग्रा॒म्याश्च॒ ये ॥
verses.iast: tasmā̎dya̱jñātsa̍rva̱huta̍ḥ । sambhṛ̍tam pṛṣadā̱jyam । pa̱śūgstāgśca̍kre vāya̱vyān̍ । ā̱ra̱ṇyāngrā̱myāśca̱ ye ॥ 9 ॥

verses.devanagari: तस्मा᳚द्य॒ज्ञाथ्स॑र्व॒हुतः॑ । ऋच॒-स्सामा॑नि जज्ञिरे । छन्दाग्ं॑सि जज्ञिरे॒ तस्मा᳚त् । यजु॒स्तस्मा॑दजायत ॥
verses.iast: tasmā̎dya̱jñātsa̍rva̱huta̍ḥ । ṛca̱s sāmā̍ni jajñire । chandā̍gṁsi jajñire̱ tasmā̎t । yaju̱s tasmā̍dajāyata ॥ 10 ॥

verses.devanagari: तस्मा॒दश्वा॑ अजायन्त । ये के चो॑भ॒याद॑तः । गावो॑ ह जज्ञिरे॒ तस्मा᳚त् । तस्मा᳚ज्जा॒ता अ॑जा॒वयः॑ ॥
verses.iast: tasmā̱daśvā̍ | ajāyanta । ye ke co̍bha̱yāda̍taḥ । gāvo̍ ha jajñire̱ tasmā̎t । tasmā̎jjā̱tā | a̍jā̱vaya̍ḥ ॥ 11 ॥

verses.devanagari: यत्पुरु॑षं॒-व्यँ॑दधुः । क॒ति॒था व्य॑कल्पयन्न् । मुख॒-ङ्किम॑स्य॒ कौ बा॒हू । कावू॒रू पादा॑वुच्येते ॥
verses.iast: yatpuru̍ṣa̱ṁu vya̍dadhuḥ । ka̱ti̱dhā vya̍kalpayan । mukha̱ṅ kima̍sya̱ kau bā̱hū । kāvū̱rū pādā̍vucyete ॥ 12 ॥

verses.devanagari: ब्रा॒ह्म॒णो᳚-ऽस्य॒ मुख॑मासीत् । बा॒हू रा॑ज॒न्यः॑ कृ॒तः । ऊ॒रू तद॑स्य॒ यद्वैश्यः॑ । प॒द्भ्याग्ं शू॒द्रो अ॑जायत ॥
verses.iast: brā̱hma̱ṇo̎'sya̱ mukha̍māsīt । bā̱hū rā̍ja̱nya̍ḥ kṛ̱taḥ । ū̱rū tada̍sya̱ yadvaiśya̍ḥ । pa̱dbhyāgṁ śū̱dro | a̍jāyata ॥ 13 ॥

verses.devanagari: च॒न्द्रमा॒ मन॑सो जा॒तः । चक्षो॒-स्सूर्यो॑ अजायत । मुखा॒दिन्द्र॑श्चा॒ग्निश्च॑ । प्रा॒णाद्वा॒युर॑जायत ॥
verses.iast: ca̱ndramā̱ mana̍so jā̱taḥ । cakṣo̱s sūryo̍ | ajāyata । mukhā̱dindra̍ścā̱gniśca̍ । prā̱ṇādvā̱yura̍jāyata ॥ 14 ॥

verses.devanagari: नाभ्या॑ आसीद॒न्तरि॑क्षम् । शी॒र् ष्णो द्यौ-स्सम॑वर्तत । प॒द्भ्या-म्भूमि॒र्दिश॒-श्श्रोत्रा᳚त् । तथा॑ लो॒काग्ं अ॑कल्पयन्न् ॥
verses.iast: nābhyā̍ | āsīda̱ntari̍kṣam । śī̱rṣṇo dyaus sama̍vartata । pa̱dbhyām bhūmi̱rdiśa̱ś śrotrā̎t । tathā̍ lo̱kāgṁ a̍kalpayan ॥ 15 ॥

verses.devanagari: वेदा॒हमे॒त-म्पुरु॑ष-म्म॒हान्तम्᳚ । आ॒दि॒त्यव॑र्ण॒-न्तम॑स॒स्तु पा॒रे । सर्वा॑णि रू॒पाणि॑ वि॒चित्य॒ धीरः॑ । नामा॑नि कृ॒त्वा-ऽभि॒वद॒न्॒, यदा-ऽऽस्ते᳚ ॥
verses.iast: vedā̱hame̱tam puru̍ṣam ma̱hāntam̎ । ā̱di̱tya va̍rṇa̱n tama̍sa̱stu pā̱re । sarvā̍ṇi rū̱pāṇi̍ vi̱citya̱ dhīra̍ḥ । nāmā̍ni kṛ̱tvā'bhi̱vada̱n yadāste̎ ॥ 16 ॥

verses.devanagari: धा॒ता पु॒रस्ता॒द्यमु॑दाज॒हार॑ । श॒क्रः प्रवि॒द्वा-न्प्र॒दिश॒श्चत॑स्रः । तमे॒वं-विँ॒द्वान॒मृत॑ इ॒ह भ॑वति । नान्यः पन्था॒ अय॑नाय विद्यते ॥
verses.iast: dhā̱tā pu̱rastā̱dyamu̍dāja̱hāra̍ । śa̱kraḥ(f) pravi̱dvānpra̱diśa̱ścata̍sraḥ । tame̱vaṁu vi̱dvāna̱mṛta̍ | i̱ha bha̍vati । nānyaḥ(f) panthā̱ | aya̍nāya vidyate ॥ 17 ॥

verses.devanagari: य॒ज्ञेन॑ य॒ज्ञम॑यजन्त दे॒वाः । तानि॒ धर्मा॑णि प्रथ॒मान्या॑सन्न् । ते ह॒ नाक॑-म्महि॒मानः॑ सचन्ते । यत्र॒ पूर्वे॑ सा॒ध्या-स्सन्ति॑ दे॒वाः ॥
verses.iast: ya̱jñena̍ ya̱jñama̍yajanta de̱vāḥ । tāni̱ dharmā̍ṇi pratha̱mānyā̍san । te ha̱ nāka̍ṁ, mahi̱māna̍s sacante । yatra̱ pūrve̍ sā̱dhyās santi̍ de̱vāḥ ॥ 18 ॥

verses.devanagari: अ॒द्भ्य-स्सम्भू॑तः पृथि॒व्यै रसा᳚च्च । वि॒श्वक॑र्मण॒-स्सम॑वर्त॒ताधि॑ । तस्य॒ त्वष्टा॑ वि॒दध॑द्रू॒पमे॑ति । तत्पुरु॑षस्य॒ विश्व॒माजा॑न॒मग्रे᳚ ॥
verses.iast: a̱dbhyas sambhū̍taḥ(f) pṛthi̱vyai rasā̎cca । vi̱śvaka̍rmaṇa̱s sama̍varta̱tādhi̍ । tasya̱ tvaṣṭā̍ vi̱dadha̍drū̱pame̍ti । tatpuru̍ṣasya̱ viśva̱mājā̍na̱magre̎ ॥ 1 ॥

verses.devanagari: वेदा॒हमे॒त-म्पुरु॑ष-म्म॒हान्तम्᳚ । आ॒दि॒त्यव॑र्ण॒-न्तम॑सः॒ पर॑स्तात् । तमे॒वं-विँ॒द्वान॒मृत॑ इ॒ह भ॑वति । नान्यः पन्था॑ विद्य॒ते-ऽय॑नाय ॥
verses.iast: vedā̱hame̱tam puru̍ṣam ma̱hāntam̎ । ā̱di̱tyava̍rṇa̱n tama̍sa̱ḥ(f) para̍stāt । tame̱vaṁu vi̱dvāna̱mṛta̍ | i̱ha bha̍vati । nānyaḥ(f) panthā̍ vidya̱te'ya̍nāya ॥ 2 ॥

verses.devanagari: प्र॒जाप॑तिश्चरति॒ गर्भे॑ अ॒न्तः । अ॒जाय॑मानो बहु॒धा विजा॑यते । तस्य॒ धीराः॒ परि॑जानन्ति॒ योनिम्᳚ । मरी॑चीना-म्प॒दमि॑च्छन्ति वे॒धसः॑ ॥
verses.iast: pra̱jāpa̍tiścarati̱ garbhe̍ | a̱ntaḥ । a̱jāya̍māno bahu̱dhā vijā̍yate । tasya̱ dhīrā̱ḥ(f) pari̍jānanti̱ yonim̎ । marī̍cīnām pa̱dami̍cchanti ve̱dhasa̍ḥ ॥ 3 ॥

verses.devanagari: यो दे॒वेभ्य॒ आत॑पति । यो दे॒वाना᳚-म्पु॒रोहि॑तः । पूर्वो॒ यो दे॒वेभ्यो॑ जा॒तः । नमो॑ रु॒चाय॒ ब्राह्म॑ये ॥
verses.iast: yo de̱vebhya̱ | āta̍pati । yo de̱vānā̎m pu̱rohi̍taḥ । pūrvo̱ yo de̱vebhyo̍ jā̱taḥ । namo̍ ru̱cāya̱ brāhma̍ye ॥ 4 ॥

verses.devanagari: रुच॑-म्ब्रा॒ह्म-ञ्ज॒नय॑न्तः । दे॒वा अग्रे॒ तद॑ब्रुवन्न् । यस्त्वै॒व-म्ब्रा᳚ह्म॒णो वि॒द्यात् । तस्य॑ दे॒वा अस॒न् वशे᳚ ॥
verses.iast: ruca̍m brā̱hmañ ja̱naya̍ntaḥ । de̱vā | agre̱ tada̍bruvan । yastvai̱vam brā̎hma̱ṇo vi̱dyāt । tasya̍ de̱vā | asa̱nvaśe̎ ॥ 5 ॥

verses.devanagari: ह्रीश्च॑ ते ल॒क्ष्मीश्च॒ पत्न्यौ᳚ । अ॒हो॒रा॒त्रे पा॒र् श्वे । नक्ष॑त्राणि रू॒पम् । अ॒श्विनौ॒ व्यात्तम्᳚ । इ॒ष्ट-म्म॑निषाण । अ॒मु-म्म॑निषाण । सर्व॑-म्मनिषाण ॥
verses.iast: hrīśca̍ te la̱kṣmīśca̱ patnyau̎ । a̱ho̱rā̱tre pā̱r·śve । nakṣa̍trāṇi rū̱pam । a̱śvinau̱ vyāttam̎ । i̱ṣṭam ma̍niṣāṇa । a̱mum ma̍niṣāṇa । sarva̍m maniṣāṇa ॥ 6 ॥

verses.devanagari: तच्छं॒-योँरावृ॑णीमहे । गा॒तुं-यँ॒ज्ञाय॑ । गा॒तुं-यँ॒ज्ञप॑तये । दैवी᳚ स्व॒स्तिर॑स्तु नः । स्व॒स्तिर्मानु॑षेभ्यः । ऊ॒र्ध्व-ञ्जि॑गातु भेष॒जम् । श-न्नो॑ अस्तु द्वि॒पदे᳚ । श-ञ्चतु॑ष्पदे ।
verses.iast: oṁ | tacha̱ṁi yorāvṛ̍ṇīmahe । gā̱tuṁi ya̱jñāya̍ । gā̱tuṁi ya̱jña pa̍taye । daivī̎ sva̱stira̍stu naḥ । sva̱stir mānu̍ṣebhyaḥ । ū̱rdhvañ ji̍gātu bheṣa̱jam । śan no̍ | astu dvi̱pade̎ । śañ catu̍ṣpade ॥

verses.devanagari: ॐ शान्ति॒-श्शान्ति॒-श्शान्तिः॑ ॥
verses.iast: oṁ | śāntiś śāntiś śānti̍ḥ ॥

overview: The Puruṣa Sūktam describes the Cosmic Person — thousand-headed, thousand-eyed, thousand-footed — who pervades the earth entirely and extends beyond it. It sets out creation as a yajña in which the Puruṣa is at once the offering, the fire and the one to whom it is offered, and from which the Vedas, the creatures, the elements and the worlds all arise.
structure: Two anuvākas. The first has eighteen verses, the second six. Both are framed by the same śānti — śaṁ yorāvṛṇīmahe — which opens the recitation and closes it again as the samāptāśīrvācanam.
universalReflection: The hymn describes a whole in which nothing stands outside: the offering, the fire, the one offering and what is made from it are all the same Person. Everything that follows in it is a description of one thing seen from different sides.

note: Kṛṣṇa Yajur Veda, Taittirīya Saṃhitā. Recited in two halves — Namakam and Chamakam — of eleven anuvākas each. Choose a half, then an anuvāka.

verses.iast: ॥ oṁ | namo bhagavate̍ rudrā̱ya ॥
oṁ | nama̍ste rudra ma̱nyava̍ | u̱tota̱ | iṣa̍ve̱ nama̍ḥ । nama̍ste | astu̱ dhanva̍ne bā̱hubhyā̍mu̱ta te̱ nama̍ḥ ॥ 1
yā ta̱ | iṣu̍ś śi̱vata̍mā śi̱vam ba̱bhūva̍ te̱ dhanu̍ḥ । śi̱vā śa̍ra̱vyā̍ yā tava̱ tayā̍ no rudra mṛḍaya ॥ 2
yā te̍ rudra śi̱vā ta̱nūragho̱rā'pā̍pakāśinī । tayā̍ nasta̱nuvā̱ śanta̍mayā̱ giri̍śantā̱bhi cā̍kaśīḥ ॥ 3
yāmiṣu̍ṅ giriśanta̱ haste̱ bibha̱rṣyasta̍ve । śi̱vāṅ gi̍ritra̱ tāṅ ku̍ru̱ mā hi̍gṁsī̱ḥ(f) puru̍ṣa̱ñ jaga̍t ॥ 4
śi̱vena̱ vaca̍sā tvā̱ giri̱śācchā̍vadāmasi । yathā̍ na̱s sarva̱mijjaga̍daya̱kṣma gṁ su̱manā̱ | asa̍t ॥ 5
adhya̍vocadadhiva̱ktā pra̍tha̱mo daivyo̍ bhi̱ṣak । ahī̍gśca̱ sarvā̎ñ ja̱mbhaya̱nth sarvā̎śca yātudhā̱nya̍ḥ ॥ 6
a̱sau yastā̱mro | a̍ru̱ṇa | u̱ta ba̱bhrus su̍ma̱ṅgala̍ḥ । ye ce̱mā gṁ ru̱drā | a̱bhito̍ di̱kṣu śri̱tās sa̍hasra̱śo'vai̍ṣā̱gṁ heḍa̍ | īmahe ॥ 7
a̱sau yo̍'va̱sarpa̍ti̱ nīla̍grīvo̱ vilo̍hitaḥ । u̱taina̍ṅ go̱pā | a̍dṛśa̱nnadṛ̍śannudahā̱rya̍ḥ । u̱taina̱ṁu viśvā̍ bhū̱tāni̱ sa dṛ̱ṣṭo mṛ̍ḍayāti naḥ ॥ 8
namo̍ | astu̱ nīla̍grīvāya sahasrā̱kṣāya̍ mī̱ḍhuṣe̎ । atho̱ ye | a̍sya̱ satvā̍no̱'han tebhyo̍'kara̱n nama̍ḥ ॥ 9

overview: Śrī Rudram is the central hymn to Rudra in the Kṛṣṇa Yajur Veda. Its first half, the Namakam, is named for the word namaḥ — salutations — which recurs throughout as Rudra is saluted in every form and in every place. Its second half, the Chamakam, is named for the phrase ca me — and for me — in which each verse asks that some good be granted.
structure: Eleven anuvākas in each half, chanted in sequence. Classes usually work through one anuvāka at a time, which is how the anuvākas are presented here.

wordMeanings.meaning: salutations — the word that names the Namakam
and for me — the phrase that names the Chamakam

universalReflection: The Namakam salutes Rudra in everything without exception — in what is pleasant and in what is feared, in the settled and in the wild. Nothing is left outside the salutation.

verses.iast: । śrī sāyīśvarāya namaḥ । hariḥ oṁ ।

verses.devanagari: जा॒तवे॑दसे सुनवाम॒ सोम॑ मरातीय॒तो निद॑हाति॒ वेदः॑ । स नः॑ पर्-ष॒दति॑ दु॒र्गाणि॒ विश्वा॑ ना॒वेव॒ सिन्धु॑-न्दुरि॒ता-ऽत्य॒ग्निः ॥
verses.iast: jā̱tave̍dase sunavāma̱ soma̍marātīya̱to nida̍hāti̱ veda̍ḥ । sa na̍ḥ(f) parṣa̱dati̍ du̱rgāṇi̱ viśvā̍ nā̱veva̱ sindhu̍n duri̱tā'tya̱gniḥ ॥

verses.devanagari: ताम॒ग्निव॑र्णा॒-न्तप॑सा ज्वल॒न्तीं-वैँ॑रोच॒नी-ङ्क॑र्मफ॒लेषु॒ जुष्टा᳚म् । दु॒र्गा-न्दे॒वीग्ं शर॑णम॒ह-म्प्रप॑द्ये सु॒तर॑सि तरसे॒ नमः॑ ॥
verses.iast: tāma̱gniva̍rṇā̱n tapa̍sā jvala̱ntīṁu vai̍roca̱nīṅ ka̍rmapha̱leṣu̱ juṣṭā̎m । du̱rgān de̱vī gṁ śara̍ṇama̱haṁ prapa̍dye su̱tara̍si tarase̱ nama̍ḥ ॥

verses.devanagari: अग्ने॒ त्व-म्पा॑रया॒ नव्यो॑ अ॒स्मान् थ्स्व॒स्तिभि॒रति॑ दु॒र्गाणि॒ विश्वा᳚ । पूश्च॑ पृ॒थ्वी ब॑हु॒ला न॑ उ॒र्वी भवा॑ तो॒काय॒ तन॑याय॒ शं योँः ॥
verses.iast: agne̱ tvam pā̍rayā̱ navyo̍ | a̱smānthsva̱stibhi̱rati̍ du̱rgāṇi̱ viśvā̎ । pūśca̍ pṛ̱thvī ba̍hu̱lā na̍ | u̱rvī bhavā̍ to̱kāya̱ tana̍yāya̱ śaṁiyoḥ ॥

verses.devanagari: विश्वा॑नि नो दु॒र्गहा॑ जातवेद॒-स्सिन्धु॒न्न ना॒वा दु॑रि॒ता-ऽति॑पर्-षि । अग्ने॑ अत्रि॒वन्मन॑सा गृणा॒नो᳚-ऽस्माक॑-म्बोध्यवि॒ता त॒नूना᳚म् ॥
verses.iast: viśvā̍ni no du̱rgahā̍ jātaveda̱s sindhu̱nna nā̱vā du̍ri̱tā'ti̍parṣi । agne̍ | atri̱vanmana̍sā gṛṇā̱no̎'smāka̍m bodhyavi̱tā ta̱nūnā̎m ॥

verses.devanagari: पृ॒त॒ना॒ जित॒ग्ं॒ सह॑मानमु॒ग्रम॒ग्निग्ं हु॑वेम पर॒माथ्स॒धस्था᳚त् । स नः॑ पर्-ष॒दति॑ दु॒र्गाणि॒ विश्वा॒ क्षाम॑द्दे॒वो अति॑ दुरि॒ता-ऽत्य॒ग्निः ॥
verses.iast: pṛ̱ta̱nā̱jita̱gṁ saha̍mānamu̱grama̱gni gṁ hu̍vema para̱māthsa̱dhasthā̎t । sa na̍ḥ(f) parṣa̱dati̍ du̱rgāṇi̱ viśvā̱ kṣāma̍dde̱vo | ati̍ duri̱tā'tya̱gniḥ ॥

verses.devanagari: प्र॒त्नोषि॑ क॒मीड्यो॑ अध्व॒रेषु॑ स॒नाच्च॒ होता॒ नव्य॑श्च॒ सत्सि॑ । स्वाञ्चा᳚-ऽग्ने त॒नुव॑-म्पि॒प्रय॑स्वा॒स्मभ्य॑-ञ्च॒ सौभ॑ग॒माय॑जस्व ॥
verses.iast: pra̱tnoṣi̍ ka̱mīḍyo̍ | adhva̱reṣu̍ sa̱nācca̱ hotā̱ navya̍śca̱ sathsi̍ । svāñcā̎gne ta̱nuva̍m pi̱ praya̍svā̱smabhya̍ñ ca̱ saubha̍ga̱māya̍jasva ॥

verses.devanagari: गोभि॒र्जुष्ट॑मयुजो॒ निषि॑क्त॒-न्तवे᳚न्द्र विष्णो॒रनु॒सञ्च॑रेम । नाक॑स्य पृ॒ष्ठम॒भि सं॒ वँसा॑नो॒ वैष्ण॑वीं-लोँ॒क इ॒ह मा॑दयन्ताम् ॥
verses.iast: gobhi̱rjuṣṭa̍ma̱yujo̱ niṣi̍kta̱n tave̎ndra viṣṇo̱ranusañca̍rema । nāka̍sya pṛ̱ṣṭhama̱bhi saṁuvasā̍no̱ vaiṣṇa̍vīṁl lo̱ka | i̱ha mā̍ dayantām ॥

overview:
A hymn to Durgā as the fire that carries one across difficulty. *Durgāṇi* means hard places or straits, and the refrain asks Agni — *jātavedas*, knower of all that is born — to ferry us over them as a boat carries one over a river. It closes with the Kātyāyanī Gāyatrī.

Read more deeply, the Sūktam describes the journey of a **perfect instrument of God** — a path exemplified by Moses — in which one must move beyond personal desires and sacrifice the self for the **mass consciousness**.

wordMeanings.meaning: she who carries one across difficulty
knower of all that is born — a name of Agni
as a boat across a river
the maiden — a name of the Goddess

universalReflection:
The Durgā Sūktam is an eternal guide for any human being seeking to become a **perfect instrument of God**, whatever their religious background. It is not a relic of the past but a living set of mantras, describing the journeys of all the great Messiahs — Moses, Jesus, Abraham.

Its core message is **purity of intent and unity in execution**. It teaches that the Divine is essentially light and fire — *Agni* — an all-pervading force that cannot be contaminated, and that is always fresh and new.

So the Sūktam asks for a shift in the level of our devotion: away from asking for mundane things — a car, a job — and towards atonement, where the seeker prays instead to become unconditionally loving and serving, just as the Divine is.

figureParallel.heading: The Sūktam and the life of Moses
figureParallel.intro: The Durgā Sūktam has been called the **essence of the life of Moses**. Though its mantras are thousands of years old, they are held to be eternally relevant to the lives of all Messiahs. The relationship is drawn through six thematic and narrative parallels.

items.title: The vision of fire on Mount Sinai
items.text: When Moses ascended Mount Sinai he encountered a pillar of fire — the same *Agni*, the fire aspect, that the Sūktam worships. Just as the Sūktam invokes the god of fire to purify intent and instinct, Moses encountered the Divine as light and fire.

items.title: The prayer for liberation and prosperity
items.text: Moses prayed for his people to be liberated from slavery and for his clan to prosper. The Sūktam mirrors this: a plea to the fire of God to help the clan cross obstacles, and to ensure abundance on Mother Earth and auspiciousness for all children and spouses.

items.title: Crossing the Red Sea
items.text: The Sūktam prays to cross the ocean of this life, using surrender to God as the boat. This links directly to the parting of the Red Sea. The mantra *vishanava* is read as a call for the Lord of Light to take the people across the sea, escaping the pursuing enemies of the Pharaoh's army.

items.title: Victory over enemies
items.text: Moses fleeing the Egyptian army corresponds to the Sūktam's invocation to defeat all enemies that obstruct one from doing God's work — a supreme consciousness called upon to destroy obstacles both outward, like the Pharaoh, and inward, like bad qualities or laziness.

items.title: The connection to Atri Maharishi
items.text: Atri Maharishi has been described as another Moses within Hinduism. The Sūktam speaks of being **like Atri** — having no attachment, and a singular focus on praying for the happiness and peace of all creation.

items.title: The Ten Commandments as obstacles
items.text: The Ten Commandments correspond to the common-sense obstacles the Sūktam helps devotees overcome. These are the lower-level obstacles — stealing, adultery, things human beings do knowingly — which the fire of the Sūktam seeks to purify.
